items.title: 1. Perioperative risk prediction tools
items.q: Discuss the role and limitations of risk prediction tools in adult non-cardiac surgery. Which tools would you use in Australia and New Zealand, and how does a tool change your management?
items.a:
> Evidence framework: current guidelines in the source key take precedence over older article treatment intervals; the original teaching explanation is retained where applicable.

> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2023, "Adult perioperative risk stratification" (Engelbrecht, Khoyratty, Reilly).

## Why use a tool

There is an ethical duty to give the patient an estimate of risk during consent. Tools can also identify patients who need enhanced monitoring, HDU or ICU, and help allocate limited resources. In the SNAP-2 study of 22,631 patients, **clinician judgement was the only documented tool in 79%**, and using a tool alongside judgement improved risk estimation.

## What makes a good tool

It should be simple, validated in the local population, and judged on two measures:

- **Discrimination:** ability to separate patients who die from those who survive (area under the ROC curve).
- **Calibration:** whether predicted risk matches observed risk. Calibration drifts over time and needs periodic **recalibration**.

## Common tools

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| ASA-PS | Not designed as a risk score but widely used; reasonable discrimination for mortality; a component of SORT and nzRISK |
| RCRI | Six-item major cardiac event estimate |
| ACS NSQIP calculator | About 1.4 million US patients, 21 variables, 30-day mortality and morbidity; proprietary; limits when applied to ANZ patients |
| P-POSSUM | Recalibrated mortality model; original POSSUM includes morbidity prediction |
| SORT | Surgical Outcome Risk Tool: 30-day mortality, includes ASA-PS and urgency |
| nzRISK | New Zealand tool predicting mortality to **2 years**, not just 30 days |

## Limitations

- Most tools predict 30-day mortality, but long-term quality of life matters to patients.
- Models can underpredict in a different population; clinicians may adjust the score.
- There is **little evidence that identifying high-risk patients improves outcomes**; the harder task is to show that risk-stratified care changes patient-centred outcomes.

## Applying the result

Use the estimate for informed consent, shared decision making (including whether to proceed), choice of monitoring, and planned postoperative disposition. Add functional capacity and frailty to the numerical score.

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives the consent and resource-allocation rationale
- Quotes that clinician judgement alone is common and a tool adds value
- Distinguishes discrimination from calibration and mentions recalibration
- Names at least four tools with a feature of each (ASA-PS, RCRI, NSQIP, P-POSSUM, SORT, nzRISK)
- Notes nzRISK includes risk to 2 years
- States the limitation that outcome benefit is unproven
- Describes how the result changes consent and disposition
